title: Third conditional: could have vs would have
question: If I had known about the delay, I ___ a different flight last night.
explanation: 'Could have + past participle' expresses a past possibility that was available but not taken. 'Could book' is a present or future form, 'had booked' belongs in an if-clause, and 'booked' is past simple.

title: Third conditional: might have
question: If the manager hadn't intervened, the argument ___ into a real fight that night.
explanation: 'Might have + past participle' expresses an uncertain past outcome in a third conditional. 'Might turn' is a present or future form, 'had turned' belongs in an if-clause and 'turned' is past simple.

title: Third conditional: contracted form
question: If we'd arrived earlier, we ___ seats near the front last night.
explanation: 'We'd' contracts 'we had'. The result clause uses 'would have + past participle', which contracts to 'would've got'. 'Would get' is a present or future form, 'had got' is past perfect and 'will have got' is a future perfect.

title: Third conditional: if-clause
question: ___ I'd checked the weather forecast, I wouldn't have left my umbrella at home.
explanation: 'If + past perfect' in the if-clause, with 'would have' in the result, makes a third conditional. 'Unless' means 'if not' and reverses the logic, 'only if' limits the condition and 'even if' says the result would have happened anyway.

title: Third conditional: wouldn't have
question: If the traffic hadn't been so bad, we ___ the flight. But it was terrible.
explanation: 'Wouldn't have + past participle' is the negative result of an unreal past: with better traffic, they would have caught the flight. 'Wouldn't miss' is a present or future form, and 'didn't miss' and 'hadn't missed' are not result-clause forms.

title: Third conditional: result clause
question: He ___ the race if he hadn't fallen at the last corner.
explanation: The result clause of the third conditional requires 'would have + past participle'. 'Would win' is a present or future form, 'had won' belongs in an if-clause and 'won' is past simple.

title: Third conditional: question with might
question: Do you think he ___ if we had invited him to the party last weekend?
explanation: 'Might have + past participle' expresses uncertainty about an unreal past outcome. 'Might come' is a present or future form, 'had come' belongs in an if-clause and 'came' is past simple.

title: Third conditional: negative result
question: If she'd seen the sign, she ___ the wrong turn.
explanation: 'Wouldn't have + past participle' is the negative result of an unreal past: she did take the wrong turn because she didn't see the sign. 'Wouldn't take' is a present or future form, and 'hadn't taken' and 'didn't take' are not result-clause forms.

title: Third conditional: would never have
question: If he hadn't moved abroad back in 2005, he ___ his wife.
explanation: 'Would never have + past participle' is the negative third conditional result. 'Would never meet' is a present or future form, 'had never met' belongs in an if-clause and 'never met' is past simple.

title: Third conditional: past perfect if-clause
question: If I ___ the answer at the time, I would have told you immediately.
explanation: The if-clause of the third conditional uses 'had + past participle'. 'Would have known' is the result-clause form, 'have known' is present perfect and 'was knowing' is not used with a state verb like 'know'.

title: Wish: past vs past perfect
question: I failed the test yesterday. I wish I ___ harder for it.
explanation: Regret about a specific completed past event requires 'wish + past perfect' (had + past participle). 'Studied' and 'would study' refer to the present or future, and 'have studied' is present perfect.

title: Wish: wish vs if only (present regret)
question: ___ I could turn back time and study languages as a child!
explanation: 'If only' is a stronger, more emotional version of 'I wish'. Both take the past simple for present unreal wishes. 'Only if' means 'on the condition that', 'even when' and 'as long as' do not express a wish.

title: Wish: would for complaints
question: I wish my neighbours ___ playing loud music. I've asked them so many times but they refuse.
explanation: 'Wish + would + base form' is used to complain about other people's annoying habits. 'Will stop', 'are stopping' and 'stop' cannot follow 'wish' in this way.

title: Wish: wouldn't for irritation
question: I wish the neighbours ___ their dog out so late every night. It keeps waking me up.
explanation: 'Wish + wouldn't + base form' complains about repeated habits. 'Don't let' (present), 'won't let' (future) and 'haven't let' (present perfect) cannot follow 'wish' in this way.

title: Wish: past perfect for deep regret
question: I wish I ___ so much money on clothes last year.
explanation: Regret about a specific past action requires 'wish + past perfect'. 'Hadn't spent' expresses the wish to undo a completed action. 'Didn't spend' and 'wouldn't spend' refer to the present or future, and 'haven't spent' is present perfect.

title: Wish: if only + past perfect
question: If only we ___ the house when it was cheap!
explanation: 'If only + past perfect (had + past participle)' expresses strong regret about a past decision. 'Bought' and 'would buy' refer to the present or future, and 'have bought' is present perfect.

title: Wish: distinguishing wish + would
question: Which sentence correctly uses 'wish + would'?
correct: I wish the bus would come on time for once.
wrong1: I wish I would be taller.
wrong2: I wish I would speak French fluently.
wrong3: I wish I would have more free time.
explanation: 'Wish + would' is for complaints about others' behaviour or external situations. We don't say 'I wish I would' about ourselves: for our own state or ability we use 'wish + past simple' or 'could'.

title: Wish: past event with be
question: I wish I ___ at the concert last night instead of staying at home.
explanation: 'Wish + past perfect' expresses regret about a past situation: 'I wish I had been at the concert.' 'Was' and 'were' refer to the present, and 'would be' is for complaints about others.

title: Wish: about the future
question: I wish tomorrow ___ a holiday, but unfortunately it's not.
explanation: For wishes about an unreal present/near-future state, use the past subjunctive. 'Were' (not 'was') is the subjunctive form. 'Will be', 'is', and 'has been' are all ungrammatical after 'wish' in this sense.

title: Wish: if only with would
question: If only the government ___ more about climate change! I keep writing to my MP but nothing happens.
explanation: 'If only + would + base form' expresses frustration about an ongoing situation. 'Does', 'is doing' and 'will do' are present or future forms that cannot follow 'if only' in this sense.

title: Modals of deduction: must have been
question: Look at her red eyes. She ___ crying before we arrived.
explanation: 'Must have + past participle' is a deduction about the past based on present evidence. 'Must be' and 'might be' refer to the present, and 'can't have been' says it was impossible.

title: Modals of deduction: can't have (past)
question: She ___ the message. Her phone was switched off all day.
explanation: 'Can't have + past participle' expresses certainty that something didn't happen in the past. 'Must have received' says the opposite, 'mustn't have' is not used for negative deductions and 'can't receive' refers to the present.

title: Modals of deduction: must vs can't (present)
question: The lights are on and I can hear music. Someone ___ home.
explanation: 'Must be' expresses a strong present deduction based on evidence. 'Can't be' says it is impossible, 'must have been' refers to the past and 'mustn't be' is a prohibition.

title: Modals of deduction: couldn't have
question: He ___ all that work in one hour yesterday. It would take a team a week.
explanation: 'Can't have + past participle' expresses disbelief about a past event. 'Must have done' says it certainly happened, 'should have done' expresses expectation or criticism, and 'mustn't have' is not used for negative deductions.

title: Modals of deduction: may have vs must have
question: She's not answering her phone. She ___ asleep, but I'm not sure.
explanation: 'May have + past participle' expresses possibility about a past event when you are not sure. 'Must have' shows certainty, 'can't have' shows impossibility and 'might fall' refers to the future.

title: Obligation in the past: had to
question: The exam was compulsory. Every student ___ take it.
explanation: 'Had to' is the past of 'have to' and expresses obligation in the past. 'Must have' needs a past participle and expresses deduction, 'has to' is present and 'mustn't' expresses prohibition.

title: Modals of deduction: can't have vs couldn't
question: He ___ been at the meeting yesterday. I saw him at the airport.
explanation: 'Can't have + past participle' deduces it was impossible that he attended. 'Must have' says he certainly attended, 'needn't have' means it wasn't necessary and 'mustn't have' is not used for negative deductions.

title: Modals of deduction: might have
question: Where's my wallet? I'm not certain where it is, but I ___ it at the restaurant.
explanation: 'Might have + past participle' expresses possibility about a past event when you are not certain. 'Must have left' shows certainty, and 'might leave' and 'might be leaving' refer to the future.

title: Modals of deduction: present must be
question: You've been working all day without eating. You ___ starving!
explanation: 'Must be' makes a present deduction about a current state based on evidence. 'Can't be' says it is impossible, 'must have been' refers to the past and 'mustn't be' is a prohibition.

title: Modals of deduction: can't be (present)
question: That ___ Sarah at the door. She's on holiday in Japan.
explanation: 'Can't be' expresses a strong present deduction that something is impossible. 'Must be' says the opposite, and 'can't have been' and 'must have been' refer to the past.

title: Relative clauses: that (things)
question: The bag ___ I left on the train had my passport in it.
explanation: In a defining relative clause about a thing, 'that' is natural. 'Who' and 'whom' are for people, and 'whose' shows possession, which doesn't fit here.

title: Relative clauses: non-defining with which
question: Our house, ___ we have lived in since 2010, needs a new roof.
explanation: Non-defining relative clauses (with commas) require 'which' for things, not 'that'. 'What' cannot introduce a relative clause and 'who' is for people.

title: Relative clauses: whose vs of which
question: That's the company ___ CEO resigned last week.
explanation: 'Whose' shows possession for both people and things. 'Who's' means 'who is'. 'Of which the CEO' is possible but very formal; 'whose' is the natural choice.

title: Relative clauses: where vs in which
question: The school ___ my children study is very close to our house.
explanation: 'Where' replaces 'in/at which' for places. 'Which' and 'that' would need a preposition ('that my children study at'), and 'whose' shows possession.

title: Relative clauses: that restriction
question: Professor Lee, ___ is from Canada, teaches four languages.
explanation: In non-defining relative clauses (with commas), 'that' cannot be used. You must use 'who' for a person who is the subject. 'Which' is for things and 'whom' is for objects.

title: Relative clauses: in which (formal)
question: 2020 was the year ___ everything changed.
explanation: 'In which' is the formal equivalent of 'when' for time expressions: 'the year in which everything changed'. 'At which' is not used with a year, 'which' alone is incomplete and 'what' cannot introduce a relative clause.

title: Relative clauses: whose for things
question: I found a tree ___ branches had been struck by lightning.
explanation: 'Whose' works for both people and things to show possession. 'Which' and 'that' cannot show possession without another word, and 'of which' would need 'the branches' to be grammatical.

title: Relative clauses: whom (formal)
question: The professor ___ I spoke to recommended this textbook.
explanation: 'Whom' is the object form, correct here because the professor receives the action (I spoke to the professor). 'Whose' shows possession, 'which' is for things and 'what' cannot introduce a relative clause.

title: Relative clauses: omitting the pronoun
question: Is this the song ___ you were singing yesterday?
explanation: When the relative pronoun is the object of the clause, it can be omitted entirely in defining clauses: 'the song you were singing'. 'Who' is for people, 'whose' shows possession and 'what' cannot introduce a relative clause.

title: Relative clauses: non-defining with where
question: I went back to Edinburgh, ___ I was born.
explanation: Non-defining clauses about places use 'where' (set off by commas). 'That' cannot be used in non-defining clauses, 'what' cannot introduce a relative clause and 'which' would need a preposition.

title: So/such...that: so + adjective
question: The suitcase was ___ heavy that I couldn't lift it.
explanation: 'So + adjective + that' is the correct pattern. 'Such' and 'such a' require a noun phrase, and 'too' is followed by 'to', not 'that'.

title: So/such...that: such + a + noun
question: It was ___ cold morning that the lake froze.
explanation: 'Such a + adjective + singular noun + that' is required. 'So a' is not valid. 'Such' without 'a' would need a plural or uncountable noun, and 'so' needs the adjective directly before 'that'.

title: So/such...that: so + many
question: There were ___ many cars on the road that we arrived two hours late.
explanation: 'So + many/much/few/little + that' is correct. 'Such' and 'such a' are not used before many/much/few/little. 'So much' doesn't collocate with the countable noun 'cars'.

title: So/such...that: so + much (uncountable)
question: He had ___ much work that he stayed at the office until midnight.
explanation: 'So + much + uncountable noun + that' is the correct pattern. 'So many' is used with countable nouns, not 'work' which is uncountable.

title: So/such...that: such + plural noun
question: They were ___ rude customers that the waiter complained to his manager.
explanation: 'Such + adjective + plural noun + that' is correct. 'Such a' is only for singular nouns. 'So' needs an adjective alone, not followed by a noun.

title: So/such...that: so + few
question: There were ___ few options that we had to accept the first offer.
explanation: 'So + few + countable noun + that' is the correct pattern. 'Such few' is not standard. 'So little' is for uncountable nouns.

title: So/such...that: so + little (uncountable)
question: We had ___ little time that we couldn't visit the museum.
explanation: 'So + little + uncountable noun + that' is correct. 'So few' is for countable nouns. 'Such a little' changes the meaning to 'a small amount of'.

title: So/such...that: such + uncountable noun
question: It was ___ awful food that we left the restaurant.
explanation: 'Such + adjective + uncountable noun + that' is correct. 'Such a' cannot precede uncountable nouns. 'So' would need the adjective alone: 'so awful that...'.

title: So/such...that: distinguishing so from such
question: He plays the guitar ___ well that he could join a band.
explanation: 'So + adverb + that' is the correct pattern. 'Such' and 'such a' must precede a noun phrase, but 'well' is an adverb, and 'too' is followed by 'to', not 'that'.

title: So/such...that: such a + positive meaning
question: It was ___ good film that we watched it twice.
explanation: 'Such a + adjective + singular countable noun + that' is the correct pattern. 'So' would work with just the adjective: 'so good that...', but not before the noun 'film'.
